title: JPMorgan Sets End-2027 Nifty Target at 29,000, Sees Up to $100 Billion Inflows
excerpt: The bank's 2027 India outlook forecasts 14 per cent earnings growth, favours domestic cyclicals over exporters, and puts its bull case at 31,000 and bear case at 22,000.
body:
• JPMorgan's base case puts the Nifty at 29,000 by the end of 2027, about 12 per cent above Thursday's close, with a bull case of 31,000 and a bear case of 22,000.
  • The bank forecasts MSCI India earnings growth of 12 per cent in 2026 and 14 per cent in 2027, and sees scope for about $100 billion in net foreign inflows if long-only funds return to benchmark weights.
  • Its 33 top picks lean to domestic cyclicals — ICICI Bank, HDFC Bank, State Bank of India and Bajaj Finance in financials; Larsen & Toubro, Adani Ports and Bharat Electronics in industrials; TVS Motor, Titan and Eternal in consumer discretionary — while it is underweight IT and materials.
  • The risks it names: three consecutive 25-basis-point RBI rate hikes, stretched valuations, a weak monsoon and El Niño-linked food inflation.

JPMorgan expects Indian stocks to rise further in 2027 after what it called the "great comeback" of 2026, setting a base-case Nifty target of 29,000 by the end of 2027 and presenting India as a potential safe haven for investors looking to diversify away from crowded AI trades, according to Reuters.

The target implies about 12 per cent upside from Thursday's closing level of 25,884.50, and it assumes a modest de-rating in valuations. The bank's bull case points to 31,000, assuming no earnings cuts and a return to the 10-year average valuation multiple; its bear case puts the index at 22,000 on slower earnings growth and a multiple below one standard deviation from its long-term average.

"Indian equities enter 2027 with support from improving corporate profitability, easing oil prices, resilient consumer demand, strong domestic credit growth, and a broadening private capex cycle."

— Rajiv Batra, JPMorgan

The earnings and flows behind the call

JPMorgan forecasts MSCI India earnings growth of 12 per cent in calendar 2026 and 14 per cent in 2027, with financials, consumer discretionary, industrials and energy the largest contributors to 2027 earnings growth. On flows, it estimates global, global ex-US, Asia ex-Japan and emerging-market funds are underweight India by 1.1, 3.0, 3.8 and 1.6 percentage points respectively; if long-only investors simply returned to benchmark weights, net inflows could reach about $100 billion. Foreign investors have already come back after selling more than $30 billion of Indian equities through October, buying about $15.5 billion so far in November, Reuters reported. India is about 15 per cent of the MSCI Emerging Markets index, against China's roughly 22 per cent, and JPMorgan argues its market scale and liquidity can absorb larger allocations than other non-AI alternatives.

What it likes, and what it avoids

The strategy favours domestic cyclicals over exporters, and quality and momentum over value. Its 33 top picks include ICICI Bank, HDFC Bank, State Bank of India and Bajaj Finance among financials; Larsen & Toubro, Adani Ports and Bharat Electronics among industrials; Divi's Laboratories, Fortis Healthcare and Apollo Hospitals in healthcare; and TVS Motor, Titan, Eternal and Tata Motors among consumer names. It is underweight IT and materials, and downgraded materials on the view that the boost from high global metal prices and a weak rupee will fade: it forecasts MSCI India Materials earnings growth slowing to 7.3 per cent in 2027 from 23.8 per cent in 2026.

The risks JPMorgan itself flags

Valuation is the first. After the November rebound, MSCI India traded at 19.7 times forward earnings, close to its 10-year average of 20.3 times, but its premium to MSCI Emerging Markets had widened to 139 per cent, about twice the historical norm of 70 per cent — so further gains need earnings growth or lower bond yields rather than richer multiples. JPMorgan expects the Reserve Bank of India to raise rates by 25 basis points at each of its next three meetings, with a meaningful risk of a 50-basis-point increase in December. It also flags fiscal constraints, a subdued monsoon and El Niño-related pressure on rural demand; food inflation reached 8.5 per cent in October, according to the report. The targets are the bank's scenarios, not forecasts of record: the 7,000-point spread between its bear and bull cases is its own measure of how much depends on earnings holding up.
